Во второй части задачи ситуация, в некот: In the second part of the problem, the situation is, in a sense, opposite: while the voltage is less than the ignition voltage, the voltage increases according to the given law. When the voltage reaches the ignition voltage, the bulb turns on and the capacitor quickly discharges down to the extinction voltage. After that, the process repeats. The bulb flashes at the moment of capacitor discharge, when the voltage suddenly drops to zero, after which the charging process repeats. The bulb flashes during the short time interval of capacitor discharge when the voltage across it suddenly falls to zero. Note that the considered circuit is a so-called relaxation oscillator. Therefore, it is necessary to carefully and thoughtfully consider how the voltage across the bulb itself changes, that is, to correctly "divide" the total voltage between the resistor and the bulb: if the bulb is off (its resistance is much greater than the resistor's resistance), then the voltage across the bulb is practically equal to the total voltage. Hence, the bulb will light up when the source voltage reaches the ignition voltage, i.e. {#0} V. When the bulb is lit, the current-voltage dependence is described by Ohm's law {0}.

Приступим к обсуждению решения данной за: Let's begin discussing the solution of this problem. First of all, it should be realized that the neon lamp acts as a kind of switch: in the low voltage range it is “off,” practically no current flows through it; at higher voltages it is “on” — its resistance becomes low. Importantly, this resistance is constant, does not depend on voltage, so in this mode the lamp behaves like an ordinary resistor, for which Ohm's law applies to the circuit segment. Crucially, these ranges overlap: in the range from {#0} to {#1} volts the lamp can be in either state. The choice depends on the “history,” on the state the lamp was in before entering this bistable range.
